## Paths in the moduli space of marked IHS manifolds

This Section is devoted to the study of the connected components of the
moduli space $\mathfrak{M}_{\Lambda}$ of marked IHS manifolds of
$K3^{[n]}$-type. In the setup of
Theorem [15](#thm_compatiblevectorbundle){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm_compatiblevectorbundle"}, the deformation of projectively
hyperholomorphic vector bundles takes place within a fixed connected
component of the moduli space of marked pairs, along generic diagonal
twistor paths. Consequently, we need to determine whether two marked IHS
manifolds of $K3^{[n]}$-type $(X_1,\eta_{X_1})$ and $(X_2,\eta_{X_2})$
belong to the same connected component of $\mathfrak{M}_{{\Lambda}}$ or,
equivalently, can be connected by parallel transport (see
Remark [26](#rmk_components){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk_components"}). To address this problem, the main tools we
employ are Eichler's criterion, which describes the orbits of primitive
elements in the $K3^{[n]}$-lattice under a certain class of isometries
(the so-called Eichler transvections), and Markman's classification of
monodromy operators for IHS manifolds of $K3^{[n]}$-type. The core
result of the Section is
Lemma [35](#markingexistence){reference-type="ref"
reference="markingexistence"}, which provides a sufficient criterion for
a IHS manifold $Y$ to admit a marking $\eta_Y$ so that $(Y,\eta_Y)$ lies
in the same connected component of $\mathfrak{M}_{\Lambda}$ as a marked
Hilbert scheme $(S^{[n]},\eta_{S^{[n]}})$, to which successfully apply
the study carried out in Section
[1.5](#sec_vanishing_twist){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec_vanishing_twist"}. This will be the starting point to
perform Construction [13](#example1){reference-type="ref"
reference="example1"}.

### Eichler's criterion

We now recall the notation and definitions needed to prove
Lemma [25](#lem_latticetheory){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem_latticetheory"}, which is an application of Eichler's
criterion to the $K3^{[n]}$-lattice.

Let $L$ be a non-degenerate lattice. For any element $w\in L$, we define
its *divisibility* $\operatorname{div}(w)$ to be the unique positive
generator of the ideal
$$(w,L) := \{w\cdot \lambda \mid \lambda \in L\} \subset \mathbb{Z}.$$
The non-degeneracy of the symmetric form induces an injective group
homomorphism $i \colon L \to L^\vee$. The quotient $A_L := L^\vee / L$
is a finite group, called the *discriminant group*. The lattice $L$ is
said to be *unimodular* if $A_L=0$.

#### Remarkable subgroups of $\mathrm{O}(L)$

Any isometry $g \in \mathrm{O}(L)$ induces a group automorphism
$\overline{g} \in \mathrm{Aut}(A_L)$. We denote by
$\widetilde{\mathrm{O}}(L)$ the subgroup of $\mathrm{O}(L)$ consisting
of those isometries whose action on the discriminant group $A_L$ is
equal to $\mathrm{id}_{A_L}$. On the other hand, we define the group
$\mathrm{O}^+(L)$ of *orientation-preserving isometries* of $L$ as the
isometries $g \in \mathrm{O}(L)$ that preserve the orientation of a
maximal positive definite subspace of $L \otimes \mathbb{R}$ (see
[@Mar11 Section 4]). This allows us to introduce
$\widetilde{\mathrm{O}}^+(L) := \widetilde{\mathrm{O}}(L) \cap \mathrm{O}^+(L) \subseteq \mathrm{O}(L)$,
which plays a key role in
Proposition [22](#prop_eichler){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop_eichler"}. Recall that the unimodular *hyperbolic plane*
is the lattice

::: center
$U = \mathbb{Z}e \oplus \mathbb{Z}f$, with $e^2 = f^2 = 0$ and
$(e,f) = 1$.
:::

::: {#prop_eichler .prop}
**Proposition 22** (*Eichler's criterion,
[@gritsenko-hulek-sankaran-abelianisation Proposition 3.3(i)]*). *Let
$L$ be an even lattice, such that $L=U_1\oplus L_1$ and
$L_1=U_2\oplus L_2$, where $U_1$ and $U_2$ denote, respectively, two
distinguished copies of the unimodular hyperbolic plane in $L$. Then, if
$v_1,v_2\in L$ are primitive elements such that*

1.  *$v_1^2=v_2^2$,*

2.  *$[v_1/\mathrm{div}(v_1)]=[v_2/\mathrm{div}(v_2)]\in A_L$,*

*there exists $\tau\in \widetilde{\mathrm{O}}^{+}(L)$ such that
$\tau(v_1)=v_2$.*
:::

Finally, we introduce the *Weyl group of reflections* defined by
$$\begin{equation}
    \label{weylgrp}
    \mathsf{W}(L) := \{ g \in \mathrm{O}^+(L) \mid \overline{g} = \pm \mathrm{id}_{A_L} \},
\end{equation}$$ which is an index $2$ extension of
$\widetilde{\mathrm{O}}^+(L)$. We refer to [@Mar08 Lemma 4.10] for a
further characterisation of $\mathsf{W}(L)$.

#### The $K3^{[n]}$-lattice {#sec_k3nlattice}

We recall that, if $S$ is a K3 surface, then $H^2(S,\mathbb{Z})$,
equipped with the intersection pairing, is abstractly isomorphic to the
unimodular lattice
$\Lambda_{K3}:= U^{\oplus 3}\oplus E_8(-1)^{\oplus 2}$ of signature
$(3,19)$, where $E_8(-1)$ is the unique even, unimodular, negative
definite lattice of rank $8$. We will refer to $\Lambda_{K3}$ as the
$K3$-*lattice*. If $X$ is an IHS manifold of $K3^{[n]}$-type, with
$n\geq 2$, then its BBF-lattice is abstractly isomorphic to the even
lattice ${\Lambda}:=\Lambda_{K3}\oplus \brak{-2(n-1)}$ of signature
$(3,20)$ and cyclic discriminant of order $2(n-1)$, where
$\brak{-2(n-1)}$ is the rank $1$ lattice generated by an element of
square $-2(n-1)$. We will refer to ${\Lambda}$ as the
*$K3^{[n]}$-lattice*.

::: rmk
*Remark 23*. The $K3^{[n]}$-lattice satisfies the hypotheses of
Proposition [22](#prop_eichler){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop_eichler"}.
:::

We choose $\delta$ to be a generator of $\brak{-2(n-1)}$ and fix, once
and for all, an identification
${\Lambda}= \Lambda_{K3} \oplus \mathbb{Z}\delta$. Then, every
$w\in{\Lambda}$ uniquely decomposes as $w=w_{K3}+m_w\delta$, where $m_w$
is an integer and $w_{K3}\in\Lambda_{K3}$.

::: {#rmk_primitiveimpliescoprime .rmk}
*Remark 24*. Note that $w$ is primitive if and only if
$\gcd(m_w,\mathrm{div}(w))=1$. This follows by observing that, since
$\mathrm{div}(w)\mid \mathrm{div}_{\Lambda_{K3}}(w_{K3})$ and
$\Lambda_{K3}$ is unimodular, we can write
$$w = \mathrm{div}(w)\, w'_{K3} + m_w \delta$$ for some
$w'_{K3}\in \Lambda_{K3}$. In particular we have that $\mathrm{div}(w)$
divides $\delta^2=-2(n-1)$.
:::

::: {#lem_latticetheory .lem}
**Lemma 25**. *Let
$w=w_{K3}+m_w\delta\in{\Lambda}=\Lambda_{K3}\oplus\mathbb{Z}\delta$ be a
primitive element. Then, for every integer
$m\equiv \pm m_w \pmod{\mathrm{div}(w)}$, there exists an isometry
$g\in\mathsf{W}({\Lambda})$ such that
$g(w)=\mathrm{div}(w)v' + m\delta$, for some primitive
$v'\in\Lambda_{K3}$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* It suffices to consider the case
$m \equiv m_w \pmod{\mathrm{div}(w)}$, since in the case
$m \equiv -m_w \pmod{\mathrm{div}(w)}$ we can post-compose with the map
$$\begin{align*}
        g\colon \Lambda_{K3}\oplus\mathbb{Z}\delta &\longrightarrow \Lambda_{K3}\oplus\mathbb{Z}\delta \\
            u_{K3}+m\delta &\longmapsto u_{K3}-m\delta
\end{align*}$$ which belongs to $\mathsf{W}({\Lambda})$. Choose
$U=\mathbb{Z}e\oplus \mathbb{Z}f\subset\Lambda_{K3}$ a hyperbolic plane,
so that $e^2=f^2=0$ and $(e,f)=1$. Since
$\widetilde{\mathrm{O}}^{+}(L)\subset\mathsf{W}(L)$, the result follows
from Proposition [22](#prop_eichler){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop_eichler"} applied to $v_1=w$ and
$v_2=\mathrm{div}(w)v' + m\delta$ where $$\begin{equation}
\label{v}
        v':=e+\left(\frac{w^2-m^2\delta^2}{2\mathrm{div}(w)^2}\right)f.
\end{equation}$$ We now verify the required conditions:

1.  We show that the coefficient of $f$ in
    [\[v\]](#v){reference-type="eqref" reference="v"} is an integer,
    showing that $v'$ is a well defined element of $\Lambda_{K3}$. In
    fact, as explained in
    Remark [24](#rmk_primitiveimpliescoprime){reference-type="ref"
    reference="rmk_primitiveimpliescoprime"}, we have a decomposition
    $w=\mathrm{div}(w)w'_{K3}+m_w\delta$ which yields
    $$\frac{w^2-m^2\delta^2}{2\mathrm{div}(w)^2}=\frac{\mathrm{div}(w)^2(w'_{K3})^2+(m_w^2-m^2)\delta^2}{2\mathrm{div}(w)^2}.$$
    Both summands in the numerator are divisible by
    $2\mathrm{div}(w)^2$. Indeed, it holds
    $2\mathrm{div}(w)^2 \mid \mathrm{div}(w)^2 (w'_{K3})^2$, and also
    $2\mathrm{div}(w)^2 \mid (m_w^2 - m^2)\delta^2$, since
    $\mathrm{div}(w) \mid (m_w - m)$ by the definition of $m$, and
    $2\mathrm{div}(w) \mid (m_w + m)\delta^2$: if $\mathrm{div}(w)$ is
    odd, then $2\mathrm{div}(w) \mid \delta^2$, while if
    $\mathrm{div}(w)$ is even, then $2 \mid (m_w + m)$ and
    $\mathrm{div}(w) \mid \delta^2$.

2.  The element $v'$ is primitive by definition (see
    [\[v\]](#v){reference-type="eqref" reference="v"}), hence $v_2$ is
    primitive by
    Remark [24](#rmk_primitiveimpliescoprime){reference-type="ref"
    reference="rmk_primitiveimpliescoprime"}, since the primitivity of
    $w$ implies $\gcd(m_w,\mathrm{div}(w)) = 1$ and consequently
    $\gcd(m,\mathrm{div}(w)) = 1$.

3.  It is straightforward to check that $v_1^2 = v_2^2$.

4.  Finally, we have an equality
    $[v_1/\mathrm{div}(v_1)]=[v_2/\mathrm{div}(v_2)]\in A_{\Lambda}$.
    The coefficients of $e$ and $f$ in $v_2$ are both multiples of
    $\mathrm{div}(w)$ and $(v_2,f)=\mathrm{div}(w)$, so we have
    $\mathrm{div}(v_2)=\mathrm{div}(w)$. Thus, we obtain
    $$\begin{align*}
                     \left[\frac{v_1}{\mathrm{div}(v_1)}\right]- \left[\frac{v_2}{\mathrm{div}(v_2)}\right]&=\left[\frac{w-v_2}{\mathrm{div}(w)}\right]=\left[\frac{\mathrm{div}(w)w'_{K3}+m_w\delta-\mathrm{div}(w)v'-m\delta}{\mathrm{div}(w)}\right]\\
                    &=\left[\frac{\mathrm{div}(w)w'_{K3}+(m_w-m)\delta-\mathrm{div}(w)v'}{\mathrm{div}(w)}\right]=0,
    \end{align*}$$ where the last equality follows from the fact that
    all summands in the numerator are divisible by $\mathrm{div}(w)$.

 ◻
:::

### Monodromy and moduli of IHS manifolds of $K3^{[n]}$-type

Let us recall that, given a deformation $p\colon \mathcal{X}\to T$ of
IHS manifolds, we can define an isometry between the BBF lattices of
each pair of fibers as parallel transport operator induced by any
continuous path $\gamma$ in $T$ connecting the two respective base
points. For any IHS manifold $X$, we denote by $\mathrm{Mon}^2(X)$ its
*monodromy group*, generated by parallel transport operators from $X$ to
itself constructed as above (see [@Mar11]).

::: {#rmk_components .rmk}
*Remark 26*. The monodromy group $\mathrm{Mon}^2(X)$ of an IHS manifold
$X$ is a deformation invariant and a finite index subgroup of
$\mathrm{O}^+(H^2(X,\mathbb{Z}))$ (see [@Ver09 Theorem 3.4] and [@Mar11
Section 4]). Moreover, it plays a key role in the characterisation of
the connected components of the moduli space $\mathfrak{M}_\Lambda$ of
marked IHS manifolds, for any suitable lattice $\Lambda$. Indeed, the
group $\mathrm{O}(\Lambda)$ acts on each connected component of
$\mathfrak{M}_\Lambda$ interchanging the markings, and the monodromy
group stabilizes each connected component under this action. More
precisely, by [@Mar11 Lemma 7.5], two marked IHS manifolds
$(X_1,\eta_1)$ and $(X_2,\eta_2)$ belong to the same connected component
of $\mathfrak{M}_\Lambda$ if and only if $\eta_2^{-1}\circ \eta_1$ is a
parallel transport operator.
:::

The monodromy group has been computed for all known deformation classes
of IHS manifolds. In the case of our interest, we have the following
description.

::: {#markman_monodromy .thm}
**Theorem 27** (*[@Mar08 Corollary 1.8], [@Mar10 Theorem 2.2]*). *Let
$X$ be an IHS manifold of $K3^{[n]}$-type, with $n\geq 2$. Then
$$\mathrm{Mon}^2(X)=\mathsf{W}(H^2(X,\mathbb{Z})).$$*
:::

::: {#rmkbeauville .rmk}
*Remark 28*. Let $g\colon \mathcal{S}\rightarrow B$ be a smooth and
proper family of $K3$ surfaces, and consider the smooth and proper
family $\bar{g}\colon \mathcal{X}\rightarrow B$ given by the relative
Douady space of $n$-points associated to $g$. Then, any parallel
transport defined in the family $\bar{g}$ preserves the canonical
decomposition
$H^2(S^{[n]},\mathbb{Z})=H^2(S,\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathbb{Z}\delta_{S^{[n]}}$,
by [@Bea83 Section 9, Lemme 2].
:::

::: rmk
*Remark 29*. The geometric decomposition of $H^2(S^{[n]},\mathbb{Z})$ in
Remark [28](#rmkbeauville){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmkbeauville"} provides a natural way to define marked pairs
of hyperkähler manifolds of $K3^{[n]}$-type starting from a marked K3
surface. Indeed, if $\eta\colon H^2(S,\mathbb{Z})\to \Lambda_{K3}$ is a
marking on a projective K3 surface $S$, then the unique isometry
$\eta_{S^{[n]}}\colon H^2(S^{[n]},\mathbb{Z})\to {\Lambda}$ restricting
to $\eta$ on $H^2(S,\mathbb{Z})$ and sending $\delta$ to the generator
of $\brak{-2(n-1)}$ defines a marking for $S^{[n]}$. If we let
$\mathfrak{M}_{K3}^0$ be the connected component of $\mathfrak{M}_{K3}$
containing the pair $(S,\eta)$ and $\mathfrak{M}_{\Lambda}^0$ be the
connected component of $\mathfrak{M}_{\Lambda}$ containing the pair
$(S^{[n]},\eta_{S^{[n]}})$, we get a well defined map $$\begin{align*}
        \theta \colon \mathfrak{M}_{K3}^0&\to \mathfrak{M}_{\Lambda}^0\\
        (S',\eta') & \to (S'^{[n]},\eta'^{[n]}).
\end{align*}$$ By Remark [28](#rmkbeauville){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmkbeauville"}, the map $\theta$ is compatible with the
respective period maps. Indeed, the embedding
$\Lambda_{K3}\hookrightarrow {\Lambda}$ induces a well defined map
$\tau\colon D_{K3}\to D_{\Lambda}$ between the respective period
domains. If we let $P\colon \mathfrak{M}_{K3} \to D_{K3}$ and
$P_{\Lambda}\colon \mathfrak{M}_{{\Lambda}}^0\to D_{\Lambda}^0$ be the
restrictions of the respective global period maps, then we get the
following commutative diagram $$\begin{equation}
\label{diag_markedK3tomarkedk3n}
\begin{tikzcd}
    {\mathfrak{M}_{K3}^0} & {\mathfrak{M}_{{\Lambda}}^0} \\
    {D_{K3}} & {D_{\Lambda}}
    \arrow["\theta", from=1-1, to=1-2]
    \arrow["{P_{K3}}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
    \arrow["P_{\Lambda}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
    \arrow["\tau", from=2-1, to=2-2].
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}$$
:::

Combining Lemma [25](#lem_latticetheory){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem_latticetheory"} with Markman's description of the
monodromy group of IHS manifolds of $K3^{[n]}$-type (see Theorem
[27](#markman_monodromy){reference-type="ref"
reference="markman_monodromy"}), we obtain the main result of this
Section, which will be used to choose suitable markings in
Section [3](#sec_mainthm){reference-type="ref" reference="sec_mainthm"}.

::: {#lem_monodromy .lem}
**Lemma 30**. *Let $S$ be a $K3$ surface and let $\delta_{S^{[n]}}$ be
half the class of the exceptional divisor on $S^{[n]}$. Let
$v=v_S+m_v\delta_{S^{[n]}}\in H^2(S^{[n]},\mathbb{Z})=H^2(S,\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathbb{Z}\delta_{S^{[n]}}$
be a primitive vector and let $m\in\mathbb{Z}$ be an integer such that
$m \equiv \pm m_v \pmod{\mathrm{div}(v)}$. Then, there exists a
monodromy operator
$g\colon H^2(S^{[n]}, \mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H^2(S^{[n]}, \mathbb{Z})$
such that $g(v)=\mathrm{div}(v) v'+m\delta_{S^{[n]}}$ with
$v'\in H^2(S,\mathbb{Z})$ primitive.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* By Lemma [25](#lem_latticetheory){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem_latticetheory"}, there exists
$g\in \mathsf{W}(H^2(S^{[n]},\mathbb{Z}))$ such that
$g(v)=\mathrm{div}(v)v'+m\delta_{S^{[n]}}$. The result follows from
$\mathsf{W}(H^2(S^{[n]},\mathbb{Z}))=\mathrm{Mon}^2(S^{[n]})$ (see
Theorem [27](#markman_monodromy){reference-type="ref"
reference="markman_monodromy"}). ◻
:::

### An invariant of primitive classes

Let $Y$ be a IHS manifold of $K3^{[n]}$-type. By definition, there
exists a $K3$ surface $S$ and a parallel transport operator
$g\colon H^2(Y,\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H^2(S^{[n]},\mathbb{Z})$. Recall
that we have a canonical decomposition
$H^2(S^{[n]},\mathbb{Z})=H^2(S,\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathbb{Z}\delta_{S^{[n]}}$.
Hence, for every primitive $w\in H^2(Y,\mathbb{Z})$, we can write
$g(w)=v+m\delta$, with $v\in H^2(S,\mathbb{Z})$. By
Remark [24](#rmk_primitiveimpliescoprime){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk_primitiveimpliescoprime"}, we have
$\gcd(m,\mathrm{div}(w))=1$. Therefore, the class $[m]$ defines an
element of $(\mathbb{Z}/\mathrm{div}(w)\mathbb{Z})^*$ and we can
consider its image in the quotient of multiplicative groups
$(\mathbb{Z}/\mathrm{div}(w)\mathbb{Z})^*/\{\pm1\}$.

::: rmk
*Remark 31*. We adopt the convention that for $d=1$ the group
$(\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z})^*/\{\pm1\}$ is the trivial group $\{1\}$. In
particular, if $\mathrm{div}(w)=1$, then every integer $m$ defines the
same class in $(\mathbb{Z}/\mathrm{div}(w)\mathbb{Z})^*/\{\pm1\}$.
:::

::: {#lem_independencyofparalleltransport .lem}
**Lemma 32**. *The class
$[m]\in(\mathbb{Z}/\mathrm{div}(w)\mathbb{Z})^*/\{\pm1\}$ does not
depend on the $K3$ surface $S$ or on the chosen parallel transport.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Consider, for $i=1,2$, two $K3$ surfaces $S_i$ and parallel
transports
$$g_i\colon H^2(Y,\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H^2(S_i^{[n]},\mathbb{Z}).$$ In
order to simplify the notation, we set $\delta_1:=\delta_{S_1^{[n]}}$
and $\delta_2:=\delta_{S_2^{[n]}}$. Notice that we have canonical
decompositions $g_1(w)=w_1+m_1\delta_1$ and $g_2(w)=w_2+m_2\delta_2$. By
the description of the discriminant group for the $K3^{[n]}$-lattice, we
obtain that
$$\left[\frac{g_i(w)}{\mathrm{div}(w)}\right]=\left[\frac{m_i\delta_i}{\mathrm{div}(w)}\right]\in A_{H^2(S_i^{[n]},\mathbb{Z})}$$
for $i=1,2$. The key fact is that, by Remark
[26](#rmk_components){reference-type="ref" reference="rmk_components"},
there is a parallel transport
$h\colon H^2(S_1,\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H^2(S_2,\mathbb{Z})$ which
induces a parallel transport
$h'\colon H^2(S_1^{[n]},\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H^2(S_2^{[n]},\mathbb{Z})$,
which preserves the canonical decompositions. In other words, we have
$h'(H^2(S_1,\mathbb{Z}))=H^2(S_2,\mathbb{Z})$ and
$h'(\delta_1)=\delta_2$. Now consider the composition
$f:=h'\circ g_1\circ g_2^{-1}$. By definition of those maps we get
$$f\left[\dfrac{m_2\delta_2}{\mathrm{div}(w)}\right]=h'\circ g_1\circ g_2^{-1}\left[\dfrac{m_2\delta_2}{\mathrm{div}(w)}\right]=h'\left[\dfrac{m_1\delta_1}{\mathrm{div}(w)}\right]=\left[\dfrac{m_1\delta_2}{\mathrm{div}(w)}\right].$$
On the other hand, the map $f$ is a monodromy operator by construction,
hence, by Theorem [27](#markman_monodromy){reference-type="ref"
reference="markman_monodromy"}, it acts as $\pm 1$ on the discriminant
group, yielding
$$f\left[\dfrac{m_2\delta_2}{\mathrm{div}(w)}\right]=\pm\left[\dfrac{m_2\delta_2}{\mathrm{div}(w)}\right].$$
We conclude that
$$0=\left[\dfrac{m_2\delta_2\pm m_1\delta_2}{\mathrm{div}(w)}\right]=\left[\dfrac{(m_2\pm m_1)\delta_2}{\mathrm{div}(w)}\right]$$
thus, since $\delta_2$ primitive, the claim holds. ◻
:::

Lemma [32](#lem_independencyofparalleltransport){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem_independencyofparalleltransport"} shows that the
following definition is independent of the choice of parallel transport.

::: {#def_invariant .df}
**Definition 33**. Let $w \in H^2(Y,\mathbb{Z})$ be a primitive class,
and let $g\colon H^2(Y,\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H^2(S^{[n]},\mathbb{Z})$
be a parallel transport operator to a Hilbert scheme, such that
$g(w)=v+m\delta_{S^{[n]}}$ under the natural decomposition. We denote by
$\ell(w)$ the class
$[m]\in(\mathbb{Z}/\mathrm{div}(w)\mathbb{Z})^*/\{\pm 1\}$, where the
latter is a quotient of multiplicative groups.
:::

The following is a straightforward consequence of
Lemma [30](#lem_monodromy){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem_monodromy"}.

::: {#lem_paralleltransporttohilb .lem}
**Lemma 34**. *Let $w\in H^2(Y,\mathbb{Z})$ be primitive and suppose
that $m$ is an integer such that $[m]= \ell(w)$ in
$(\mathbb{Z}/\mathrm{div}(w)\mathbb{Z})^*/\{\pm 1\}$. Then there exists
a $K3$ surface $S$ and a parallel transport
$g\colon H^2(Y,\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H^2(S^{[n]},\mathbb{Z})$ such that
$g(w)=\mathrm{div}(w) w'+m\delta_{S^{[n]}}$ with
$w'\in H^2(S,\mathbb{Z})$ primitive.*
:::

We conclude the Section with a geometric application of Lemma
[34](#lem_paralleltransporttohilb){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem_paralleltransporttohilb"} that will be crucial in the
next constructions. Fix the usual identification
${\Lambda}=\Lambda_{K3}\oplus\mathbb{Z}\delta$.

::: {#markingexistence .lem}
**Lemma 35**. *Let $Y$ be an IHS manifold of $K3^{[n]}$-type. Let
$w\in H^2(Y,\mathbb{Z})$ be primitive and $m$ be a positive integer such
that $w^2>-m^2(2n-2)$ and $[m]=\ell(w)$ in
$(\mathbb{Z}/\mathrm{div}(w)\mathbb{Z})^*/\{\pm 1\}$. Then there exists
a marking $\eta_Y\colon H^2(Y,\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow{\Lambda}$ and
$(S,\eta_S)\in\mathfrak{M}_{\Lambda_{K3}}$ a marked $K3$ surface such
that*

1.  *$(Y,\eta_Y)$ and $(S^{[n]},\eta_{S^{[n]}})$ lie in the same
    connected component of $\mathfrak{M}_{\Lambda}$, where
    $\eta_{S^{[n]}}$ is the natural marking induced by $\eta_S$;*

2.  *$\eta_Y(w)=\mathrm{div}(w)v+m\delta\in{\Lambda}$, where
    $v\in\Lambda_{K3}$ is primitive.*

3.  *$\mathrm{Pic}(S)\cong \mathbb{Z}\eta_S^{-1}(v)$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* By
Lemma [34](#lem_paralleltransporttohilb){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem_paralleltransporttohilb"}, there exists a $K3$ surface
$S'$ and a parallel transport operator
$g\colon H^2(Y,\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow H^2(S'^{[n]},\mathbb{Z})$ such
that $g(w)=\mathrm{div}(w) w'+m\delta_{S'^{[n]}}$ with
$w'\in H^2(S',\mathbb{Z})$ primitive. Choose any marking $\eta_{S'}$ on
the $K3$ surface $S'$ and define $v:=\eta_{S'}(w')$. Then, we can
consider $(S'^{[n]},\eta_{S'^{[n]}}):=\theta(S',\eta_{S'})$, following
the notation of
Diagram [\[diag_markedK3tomarkedk3n\]](#diag_markedK3tomarkedk3n){reference-type="ref"
reference="diag_markedK3tomarkedk3n"}. By assumption $w^2+m^2(2n-2)>0$,
we obtain $(w')^2>0$ and hence $v^2>0$. A consequence of the
surjectivity of the period map for $K3$ surfaces (see [@HuyK3 Corollary
14.3.1]), there is some $(S,\eta_S)$ in the same connected component of
$(S',\eta_{S'})$ such that
$\mathrm{Pic}(S)\cong \mathbb{Z}\eta_S^{-1}(v)$. Then
$(S^{[n]},\eta_{S^{[n]}}):=\theta(S,\eta_S)$ is in the same connected
component as $(S'^{[n]},\eta_{S'^{[n]}})$. Therefore, the result follows
by setting $\eta_Y:=\eta_{S'^{[n]}}\circ g$. This implies that
$(Y,\eta_Y)$ and $(S'^{[n]},\eta_{S'^{[n]}})$ are in the same connected
component and therefore also $(Y,\eta_Y)$ and $(S^{[n]},\eta_{S^{[n]}})$
are. ◻
:::

For completeness, we include here a Lemma describing the orbit of the
$K3$-part under monodromy, once the coefficient of $\delta_{S^{[n]}}$ is
fixed.

::: lem
**Lemma 36**. *Let $S$ be a $K3$ surface. Let
$w=w_{K3}+m\delta_{S^{[n]}}\in H^2(S^{[n]},\mathbb{Z})=H^2(S,\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathbb{Z}\delta_{S^{[n]}}$
be primitive. Pick $w'_{K3}\in H^2(S,\mathbb{Z})$. Then there exists
$g\in \mathrm{Mon}^2(S^{[n]})$ such that
$g(w)=w'_{K3}+m\delta_{S^{[n]}}$ if and only if the following three
conditions hold:*

1.  *$(w'_{K3})^2=(w_{K3})^2$;*

2.  *$\gcd(\mathrm{div}(w'_{K3}),m)=1$;*

3.  *$\mathrm{div}(w)=\gcd(\mathrm{div}(w'_{K3}),2n-2)$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The conditions are easily seen to be necessary, since a
monodromy operator preserves squares, primitivity and divisibility. They
are also sufficient, by Eichler's criterion
Proposition [22](#prop_eichler){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop_eichler"} . ◻
:::

## Moduli spaces of modular vector bundles

In this Section, we present the proof of our main result.

::: {#thm_main .thm}
**Theorem 37**. *Let $n\geq 2$ be an integer, let $Y$ be a projective
IHS manifold of $K3^{[n]}$-type and let $w \in \mathrm{NS}(Y)$ be a
primitive class. If $\mathrm{div}(w)$ is odd, consider a positive even
integer $r$ such that :*

1.  *$\left[\frac{r}{2}\right]=\ell(w)\in (\mathbb{Z}/\mathrm{div}(w)\mathbb{Z})^*/\{\pm 1\}$;*

2.  *$\frac{w^2}{2r}+ \frac{r}{4}(n-1)$ is a positive integer;*

3.  *$\frac{w^2}{2r}+ \frac{r}{4}(n-1)$ is coprime with $r$.*

*If $\mathrm{div}(w)$ is even, consider a positive integer $r\geq 3$
such that:*

1.  *$[r]=\ell(w)\in (\mathbb{Z}/\mathrm{div}(w)\mathbb{Z})^*/\{\pm 1\}$;*

2.  *$\frac{w^2}{2r} + r(n-1)$ is a positive integer;*

3.  *$\frac{w^2}{2r}$ is coprime with $r$.*

*Then, there exists a polarisation $H$ on $Y$ and a connected component
$X$ of the moduli space $M_{Y,H}$ of Gieseker $H$-semistable sheaves on
$Y$, such that*

1.  *$X$ is an IHS manifold of $K3^{[n]}$-type.*

2.  *$X$ parametrises $\mu_H$-stable modular vector bundles $E$ on $Y$
    with the following invariants:*

    ::: minipage
    *$$\begin{equation*}
            c_1(E)= \bigg\{\begin{array}{ll}
               r^{n-1}n! w  & \textit{if }\mathrm{div}(w) \textit{ is odd} \\
               r^{n-1}n! \frac{w}{2}  & \textit{if }\mathrm{div}(w) \textit{ is even}
            \end{array}
    \end{equation*}$$*
    :::

    ::: minipage
    *$$\begin{align*}
           \mathrm{rk}(E)&= r^n n!\\
            \Delta(E) &= \frac{(r^n n!)^2}{12}c_2(Y).
    \end{align*}$$*
    :::

3.  *The Fourier-Mukai transform
    $$\Phi_\mathcal{E}\colon \mathrm{D}^b(X) \to \mathrm{D}^b(Y)$$ with
    kernel $\mathcal{E}$ is an equivalence, where $\mathcal{E}$ is a
    universal family on $X\times Y$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof of Theorem [37](#thm_main){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm_main"} for $\mathrm{div}(w)$ odd.* The idea of the proof
is to construct the universal family $(\mathcal{E},\alpha_\mathcal{E})$
on $X \times Y$, as in
Theorem [15](#thm_compatiblevectorbundle){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm_compatiblevectorbundle"}, in such a way that the twist
vanishes. Thus $\mathcal{E}$ is a family of untwisted vector bundles on
$Y$. We then prove that the fibers over points $x \in X$ are stable with
respect to a suitable polarisation and show that the induced map from
$X$ to the moduli space is an isomorphism onto a connected component.

By [\[a\]](#a){reference-type="ref" reference="a"} and
[\[b\]](#b){reference-type="ref" reference="b"} we have
$\ell(w)=\left[r/2\right]$ and
$w^2 > -\frac{r}{4}(n-1)\cdot 2r = -(r/2)^2(2n-2)$, hence we can apply
Lemma [35](#markingexistence){reference-type="ref"
reference="markingexistence"} with $m = r/2$. Therefore, there exists a
marked Hilbert scheme $(S^{[n]},\eta_{S^{[n]}})$ and a marking
$\eta_Y\colon H^2(Y,\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow {\Lambda}$, such that

1.  $(Y,\eta_Y)$ and $(S^{[n]},\eta_{S^{[n]}})$ lie in the same
    connected component of $\mathfrak{M}_{\Lambda}$, which we denote by
    $\mathfrak{M}^\circ_{\Lambda}$;

2.  []{#2 label="2"}
    $\eta_Y(w)=\mathrm{div}(w)v-\frac{r}{2}\delta\in{\Lambda}$, where
    $v\in\Lambda_{K3}$ is primitive.

3.  []{#3 label="3"} $\mathrm{Pic}(S)\cong \mathbb{Z}h$, where
    $h:=\eta_S^{-1}(v)$.

By [\[b\]](#b){reference-type="ref" reference="b"} and
[\[2\]](#2){reference-type="ref" reference="2"} the isotropic Mukai
vector $$\begin{equation}
\label{Mukai_odd}
    u:= \left(r,\;\mathrm{div}(w)h,\;\frac{\mathrm{div}(w)^2h^2}{2r}\right) \in H^{\ast}(S,\mathbb{Z})
\end{equation}$$ is well-defined. Moreover, by
[\[a\]](#a){reference-type="ref" reference="a"} and
[\[c\]](#c){reference-type="ref" reference="c"} we have
$$\gcd(r,\;\mathrm{div}(w))=1=\gcd\left(r,\;\frac{\mathrm{div}(w)^2h^2}{2r}\right),$$
in particular $u$ is primitive. Hence, we can perform
Construction [13](#example1){reference-type="ref" reference="example1"},
which yields a projectively hyperholomorphic vector bundle
$\mathcal{U}^{[n]} \in \mathrm{Coh}(M^{[n]}\times S^{[n]})$, where
$M:= M_S(u)$ is another $K3$ surface. Without loss of generality, in the
construction we can choose
$\mathcal{U}^{[n]}\in\mathrm{Coh}(M^{[n]}\times S^{[n]})$ as in
Remark [19](#rmk_nicotranquillo){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk_nicotranquillo"}. Moreover, there exist a marking
$\eta_{M^{[n]}}$ and a rational isometry
${\psi^{[n]}}\colon \Lambda_{K3^{[n]},\mathbb{Q}} \to \Lambda_{K3^{[n]},\mathbb{Q}}$
such that $\eta_{S^{[n]}} \circ {\psi^{[n]}}\circ \eta_{M^{[n]}}$ is a
rational Hodge isometry sending some Kähler class to a Kähler class (see
Section [1.5](#sec_vanishing_twist){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec_vanishing_twist"}). We denote by
$\mathfrak{M}^\circ_{{\psi^{[n]}}}$ the connected component of the
moduli space of marked pairs containing
$(M^{[n]},\eta_{M^{[n]}},S^{[n]},\eta_{S^{[n]}})$.

Since $(Y,\eta_Y)$ and $(S^{[n]},\eta_{S^{[n]}})$ both lie in
$\mathfrak{M}^\circ_{\Lambda}$, by
Lemma [14](#lem_pisurj){reference-type="ref" reference="lem_pisurj"}
there exists
$(X,\eta_X,Y,\eta_Y) \in \mathfrak{M}^\circ_{{\psi^{[n]}}}$. As a
consequence, by
Theorem [15](#thm_compatiblevectorbundle){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm_compatiblevectorbundle"}, there exist a split Kähler
class $\omega_{X\times Y}$ and a projectively
$\omega_{X\times Y}$-stable hyperholomorphic vector bundle
$(\mathcal{E},\alpha_\mathcal{E})$ on $X\times Y$, which is the kernel
of a twisted Fourier--Mukai equivalence
$$\phi_{\mathcal{E}}\colon \mathrm{D}^b(X,\alpha_X^{-1}) \to \mathrm{D}^b(Y,\alpha_Y),$$
where
$\alpha_\mathcal{E}= \alpha_X + \alpha_Y \in \mathrm{Br}(X\times Y) = \mathrm{Br}(X) \oplus \mathrm{Br}(Y)$.

Since
$\eta_Y^{-1}\circ\eta_{S^{[n]}}c_1\left(\mathcal{U}^{[n]}|_{\{x\}\times Y}\right)\in\mathbb{Q}w\subset\mathrm{Pic}_{\mathbb{Q}}(Y)$,
by Lemma [18](#lem_sufficientcondition){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem_sufficientcondition"}, we have $\alpha_X=0$ and
$\alpha_Y=0$. By
Theorem [15](#thm_compatiblevectorbundle){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm_compatiblevectorbundle"} (3), together with
Remark [11](#rmk_trasp_c1){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk_trasp_c1"}, we conclude that the fibers, up to tensoring
with a holomorphic line bundle $L\in\mathrm{Pic}(Y)$ satisfy
$$\begin{equation*}
    c_1(\mathcal{E}_x)= 
           r^{n-1}n! w
\end{equation*}$$ The computation of $\Delta(\mathcal{E}_x)$ follows
from the fact that $\kappa(\mathcal{E})$ is obtained from parallel
transport from $\kappa(\mathcal{U}^{[n]})$ and
Equations [\[rank1\]](#rank1){reference-type="eqref"
reference="rank1"},[\[c11\]](#c11){reference-type="eqref"
reference="c11"},[\[eq_modularity1\]](#eq_modularity1){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq_modularity1"}. As a consequence, for all $x \in X$, the
bundle $\mathcal{E}|_{\{x\}\times Y}$ is $\omega_Y$-slope stable.
Indeed, by Lemma [53](#lem_fibersarestable){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem_fibersarestable"}, the restriction
$\mathcal{E}|_{\{x\}\times Y}$ is $\omega_Y$-slope polystable; moreover,
it is simple by [@caldararu-thesis Theorem 3.2.1]. By
Lemma [56](#lem_omegaimpliesH){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem_omegaimpliesH"}, there exists an ample divisor
$H \in \mathrm{Pic}(Y)$ such that $\mathcal{E}|_{\{x\}\times Y}$ is
$H$-slope stable, for all $x\in X$. We conclude by
Lemma [16](#lem_Ymodulisp){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem_Ymodulisp"} that $X$ can be identified with a connected
component of the moduli space of Gieseker $H$-semistable sheaves. ◻
:::

::: proof
*Proof of Theorem [37](#thm_main){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm_main"} for $\mathrm{div}(w)$ even.* The idea of the proof
is the same as in the previous case; we explain here the differences. By
[\[a2\]](#a2){reference-type="ref" reference="a2"} and
[\[b2\]](#b2){reference-type="ref" reference="b2"} we have
$\ell(w) = [r]$ and $w^2 > -r^2(2n-2)$, so that we can apply
Lemma [35](#markingexistence){reference-type="ref"
reference="markingexistence"} with $m = r$. Hence, there exist a marked
Hilbert scheme $(S^{[n]},\eta_{S^{[n]}})$ and a marking
$\eta_Y \colon H^2(Y,\mathbb{Z}) \to {\Lambda}$ such that

1.  $(Y,\eta_Y)$ and $(S^{[n]},\eta_{S^{[n]}})$ lie in the same
    connected component of $\mathfrak{M}_{\Lambda}$, which we denote by
    $\mathfrak{M}^\circ_{\Lambda}$;

2.  []{#2' label="2'"}
    $\eta_Y(w) = \mathrm{div}(w)v - r\delta \in {\Lambda}$, where
    $v \in \Lambda_{K3}$ is primitive;

3.  $\mathrm{Pic}(S) \cong \mathbb{Z}h$, where $h := \eta_S^{-1}(v)$.

As in the previous case, we can perform
Construction [13](#example1){reference-type="ref" reference="example1"},

\label{Mukai_even}
    u := \left(r,\;\frac{\mathrm{div}(w)}{2}h,\;\frac{\mathrm{div}(w)^2 h^2}{8r}\right) \in H^{\ast}(S,\mathbb{Z}),
\end{equation}$$ which can be shown to be well-defined, primitive,
isotropic, and such that
$$\gcd\left(r,\; \frac{\mathrm{div}(w)}{2}\right) = 1= \gcd\left(r,\; \frac{\mathrm{div}(w)^2 h^2}{8r}\right),$$
using [\[2\'\]](#2'){reference-type="ref" reference="2'"},
[\[a2\]](#a2){reference-type="ref" reference="a2"},
[\[b2\]](#b2){reference-type="ref" reference="b2"} and
[\[c2\]](#c2){reference-type="ref" reference="c2"}. The rest of the

### Corollaries of the main result

In this Section, we apply results of Markman [@markman],
Taelman [@tae23] and Huybrechts--Stellari [@paolo_huy] to compare the
Hodge structures of the moduli spaces involved in Theorem
[37](#thm_main){reference-type="ref" reference="thm_main"}.

We recall that the rational cohomology of any smooth projective variety
$Z$ is naturally equipped with a lattice structure, given by the Mukai
pairing, and with the following weight $0$ Hodge structure
$$\begin{equation}
    \label{HSuntwisted} H^{-k,k}(Z):= \bigoplus_{p-q=k} H^{p,q}(Z),
\end{equation}$$ for any $k= -\dim(Z),\dots, \dim(Z)$ (see [@Huy03
Section 6.1]).

From Theorem [37](#thm_main){reference-type="ref" reference="thm_main"},
combined with [@Huy03 Proposition 5.39, 5.44], we deduce the following.

::: {#cor_1 .cor}
**Corollary 39**. *In the setup of Theorem
[37](#thm_main){reference-type="ref" reference="thm_main"}, the
cohomological Fourier--Mukai transform $$\begin{align*}
        \tau_{\mathcal{E}}\colon H^{\ast}(X,\mathbb{Q})&\longrightarrow H^{\ast}(Y,\mathbb{Q})\\
        \alpha &\longmapsto p_{Y,*}\left(p_X^*\alpha\cdot\mathrm{ch}(\mathcal{E})\sqrt{\operatorname{td}_{X\times Y}}\right)
\end{align*}$$ is an isometry with respect to the Mukai pairing and an
isomorphism of weight $0$ Hodge structures, with respect to
([\[HSuntwisted\]](#HSuntwisted){reference-type="ref"
reference="HSuntwisted"}).*
:::

Next, we deal with the twisted case. Let $Z$ be a smooth projective
variety over the complex numbers such that
$H^3(Z,\mathbb{Z})_{\mathrm{tors}}=0$. Following Huybrechts--Stellari
[@paolo_huy], we recall the construction of twisted Chern characters for
twisted coherent sheaves on $Z$. Let
$\alpha\in \mathrm{Br}(Z)=H^2_{\mathrm{an}}(Z,\mathcal{O}_Z^\times)_{\mathrm{tors}}$
and let $B_Z\in H^2(Z,\mathbb{Q})$ be a $B$-field lift of $\alpha$, i.e.
a class such that $\exp(B_Z^{0,2})=\alpha$. Let $\{\alpha_{ijk}\}$ be a
cocycle representing $\alpha$ with respect to a sufficiently fine
analytic open cover $\{U_i\}$ of $Z$. Since the sheaf
$\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ of smooth functions is acyclic, there exist
smooth functions $b_{ij}\in \Gamma(U_i\cap U_j, \mathcal{C}^{\infty})$
such that $\alpha_{ijk}=\exp{(-b_{ij}+b_{ik}-b_{jk})}$. If $E$ is an
$\alpha$-twisted coherent sheaf with transition isomorphisms
$\phi_{ij}:{E_i}_{|U_i\cap U_j}\to {E_j}_{|U_{i}\cap U_j}$, the modified
transition maps $\phi'_{ij}=\exp(b_{ij})\phi_{ij}$ define an untwisted
sheaf $E'=(E_{i},\phi'_{ij})$. Following Huybrechts--Stellari, one
defines $\mathrm{ch}^{B_Z}(E):=\mathrm{ch}(E')$ (see [@paolo_huy
Proposition 1.2]).

We can generalise the weight $0$ Hodge structure defined in
([\[HSuntwisted\]](#HSuntwisted){reference-type="ref"
reference="HSuntwisted"}) to the twisted case as follows:
$$\begin{equation}
\label{eq_defzeroHstru}
    H^{-k,k,B_Z}(Z):=\exp(B_Z)\left(\bigoplus_{p-q=k}H^{p,q}(Z)\right).
\end{equation}$$ Accordingly, we can then state the following.

::: {#huystellari .prop}
**Proposition 40** ([@paolo_huy Section 4, 4) and 5)]). *A twisted
derived equivalence
$\mathrm{D}^b(X,\alpha_X^{-1})\to \mathrm{D}^b(Y,\alpha_Y)$ with
Fourier-Mukai kernel
$(\mathcal{E},\mathrm{pr}_X^*\alpha_X+\mathrm{pr}_Y^*{\alpha_Y})$ with
$\alpha_X\in \mathrm{Br}(X)$ and $\alpha_Y\in\mathrm{Br}(Y)$, induces an
isomorphism
$$\tau_{\mathcal{E}}\colon H^*(X,\mathbb{Q})\to H^*(Y,\mathbb{Q})$$
defined by the class
$\mathrm{ch}^{-B_X+B_Y}(\mathcal{E})\sqrt{\operatorname{td}_{X\times Y}}$,
where $B_X$ (resp. $B_Y$) is a $B$-field for the Brauer class $\alpha_X$
(resp. $\alpha_Y$). This isomorphism is an isometry with respect to the
Mukai pairing and an isomorphism of weight $0$ Hodge structures, with
respect to
 [\[eq_defzeroHstru\]](#eq_defzeroHstru){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq_defzeroHstru"}.*
:::

Proposition [40](#huystellari){reference-type="ref"
reference="huystellari"} naturally applies in the setting of
Theorem [15](#thm_compatiblevectorbundle){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm_compatiblevectorbundle"}, since we have a twisted derived
equivalence
$\mathrm{D}^b(X,\alpha_X^{-1})\rightarrow\mathrm{D}^b(Y,\alpha_Y)$ and
explicit $B$-fields for $\alpha_X$ and $\alpha_Y$.

::: {#rmk_iso_nonfine .rmk}
*Remark 41*. In the setup of
Remark [21](#rmk_nonfinemoduli){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk_nonfinemoduli"}, there is an isomorphism
$$\tau_{\mathcal{E}}\colon H^*(X,\mathbb{Q})\to H^*(Y,\mathbb{Q})$$
induced by the class $\mathrm{ch}^{-\mathrm{pr}_X^*B_X}(\mathcal{E})$
where $B_X$ is a $B$-field for the Brauer class $\alpha_X$. This
isomorphism preserves the Mukai pairing and suitable Hodge structures,
as in Proposition [40](#huystellari){reference-type="ref"
reference="huystellari"}.
:::

In the setup of
Theorem [15](#thm_compatiblevectorbundle){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm_compatiblevectorbundle"}, building on the work of
[@tae23], Markman constructs a rational Hodge isometry
$H^2(X,\mathbb{Q})\rightarrow H^2(Y,\mathbb{Q})$. In the next result, we
consider the pure Hodge structure on the second cohomology group of a
IHS manifold and the Beauville--Bogomolov--Fujiki form.

::: {#cor_2 .cor}
**Corollary 42** ([@markman Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 1.1]). *In the setup
of Theorem [37](#thm_main){reference-type="ref" reference="thm_main"}
and Theorem [15](#thm_compatiblevectorbundle){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm_compatiblevectorbundle"} we have a rational isometry and
isomorphism of weight $2$ Hodge structures $$\begin{equation}
         \psi_{\mathcal{E}}\colon H^2(X,\mathbb{Q})\to H^2(Y,\mathbb{Q})
\end{equation}$$ which is a rational multiple of the following
composition $$\begin{equation}
        H^2(X,\mathbb{Q})\xrightarrow{\cup c_2(X)^{n-1}}H^{4n-2}(X,\mathbb{Q})\overset{\phi_{\mathcal{E}}}{\longrightarrow}H^2(Y,\mathbb{Q})
\end{equation}$$ where $\phi_{\mathcal{E}}$ the correspondence defined
by the class $\kappa(\mathcal{E})\sqrt{\operatorname{td}_{X\times Y}}$
(see [\[eq_def_kappa\]](#eq_def_kappa){reference-type="eqref"
reference="eq_def_kappa"}).*
:::

Finally, we prove that the component $X$ of the moduli space in
Theorem [37](#thm_main){reference-type="ref" reference="thm_main"} comes
naturally equipped with a primitive class in $H^2(X,\mathbb{Z})$. In
what follows, we use the notation introduced in Subsection
[1.5](#sec_vanishing_twist){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec_vanishing_twist"}.

::: {#integral_primitive .cor}
**Corollary 43**. *In the setup of Theorem
[37](#thm_main){reference-type="ref" reference="thm_main"}, the class
$\psi_{\mathcal{E}}^{-1}(w)\in H^2(X,\mathbb{Q})$ is integral and
primitive.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* We treat only the case where $\mathrm{div}(w)$ is odd, since
the other case is similar.

In this case $r$ is even. By [\[2\]](#2){reference-type="ref"
reference="2"} and [\[3\]](#3){reference-type="ref" reference="3"}, we
obtain
$$\psi_{\mathcal{U}^{[n]}}^{-1}\circ\eta_{S^{[n]}}^{-1}\circ\eta_Y(w)=\psi_{\mathcal{U}^{[n]}}^{-1}\left(\mathrm{div}(w)h-\dfrac{r}{2}\delta_{S^{[n]}}\right)=\mathrm{div}(w)\widehat{h}-\dfrac{r}{2}\delta_{M^{[n]}}\in H^2(M^{[n]},\mathbb{Z})$$
The class $\mathrm{div}(w)\widehat{h}-\dfrac{r}{2}\delta_{M^{[n]}}$ is
primitive, since $\gcd(\mathrm{div}(w),r)=1$. By
[\[commutation_markings\]](#commutation_markings){reference-type="eqref"
reference="commutation_markings"}, it follows that
$$\psi_{\mathcal{E}}^{-1}(w)=\eta_X^{-1}\circ\eta_{M^{[n]}}\circ\psi_{\mathcal{U}^{[n]}}^{-1}\circ\eta_{S^{[n]}}^{-1}\circ\eta_Y(w)=\eta_X^{-1}\circ\eta_{M^{[n]}}\left(\mathrm{div}(w)\widehat{h}-\dfrac{r}{2}\delta_{M^{[n]}}\right).$$
Therefore $\psi_{\mathcal{E}}^{-1}(w)$ is integral and primitive. ◻
:::

## Examples of moduli spaces

In this Section, we give examples to which
Theorem [37](#thm_main){reference-type="ref" reference="thm_main"}
applies. More precisely, for every $n$ there are infinitely many
polarisation types such that every polarised IHS $(Y,w)$ of
$K3^{[n]}$-type, with $w$ of one of those types, satisfies the
assumption of Theorem [37](#thm_main){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm_main"}. This yields examples of smooth components of
moduli spaces of modular vector bundles on IHS varieties of every even
dimension.

Let $^{n}\mathcal{M}_m^{(\gamma)}$ denote the coarse moduli space of
polarised IHS manifolds $(Y,w)$ of $K3^{[n]}$-type such that $w$ is
ample, of divisibility $\mathrm{div}(w)=\gamma$, and $w^2=2m$ (see
[@GHS_moduli_IHS Theorem 1.5] for its construction). This moduli space
is quasi-projective. Moreover, by [@apost_moduli_red], if either
$\gamma=1$, or $\gamma=2$ and $n+m\equiv 1\pmod{4}$, then
$^{n}\mathcal{M}_m^{(\gamma)}$ is irreducible of dimension 20 (see also
[@olivier_HK Theorem 3.5]). By the works of O'Grady, Beauville--Donagi,
Debarre--Voisin and Iliev--Ranestad, the general element of
$^{2}\mathcal{M}_m^{(\gamma)}$ admits an explicit construction for
$(\gamma,m)=(1,1), (2,3), (2,11), (2,19)$. We refer to [@olivier_HK
§3.6.1] for an overview. In what follows, we verify that these four
cases are covered by Theorem [37](#thm_main){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm_main"} (see
Corollaries [45](#cor_EPWsextic){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor_EPWsextic"} and [47](#cor_BD_DV_IR){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor_BD_DV_IR"}). On the other hand,
Theorem [37](#thm_main){reference-type="ref" reference="thm_main"} does
not apply to the LLSvS eightfolds or to the EPW cube sixfolds (see
[@LLSvS] and [@EPWcubes]).

### Divisibility one

Let us fix a polarised IHS variety
$(Y,w)\in {}^{n}\mathcal{M}_{m}^{(1)}$ with polarisation of divisibility
one. This is irreducible of dimension 20. Let us fix
$r'\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ such that

- $k:=\dfrac{w^2}{4r'}+\dfrac{r'(n-1)}{2}\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$

- $(k,2r')=1$.

It is then easy to observe that choosing $r:=2r'$ we can always verify
the assumptions of Theorem [37](#thm_main){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm_main"}. Solving in $w^2$ we get $$w^2=2r'(2k-r'(n-1)).$$
Therefore, starting from $r'$, we can choose infinitely many $k$ and $w$
satisfying those assumptions.

::: {#cor_div1 .cor}
**Corollary 44**. *Let $r',k\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ such that
$(k,2r')=1$ and $2r'(2k-r'(n-1))\geq 1$. Then, for any
$(Y,w)\in {}^{n}\mathcal{M}_{w^2/2}^{(1)}$ with $w^2=2r'(2k-r'(n-1))$
there is a polarisation $H$ on $Y$ and a connected component $X$ of the
moduli space $M_{Y,H}$ of Gieseker $H$-semistable sheaves on $Y$ such
that*

- *$X$ parametrises $\mu_H$-stable modular vector bundles $E$ with
  $$rk(E)=(2r')^n n! \qquad c_1(E)=(2r')^{n-1}n!w \qquad \Delta(E)=\frac{((2r')^n n!)^2}{12}c_2(Y)$$*

- *$X$ and $Y$ are derived equivalent.*

*Moreover, if $\mathrm{Pic}(Y)\cong \mathbb{Z}w$ then
$(X,\psi_{\mathcal{E}}^{-1}(w))\in {}^{n}\mathcal{M}_{w^2/2}^{(1)}$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* For the first two claims, it is enough to notice that, given
$r',k\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ such that $(k,2r')=1$ and
$2r'(2k-r'(n-1))\geq 1$, the assumptions of Theorem
[37](#thm_main){reference-type="ref" reference="thm_main"} are
satisfied.

Notice that $\psi_{\mathcal{E}}^{-1}(w)$ is integral and primitive, due
to Corollary [43](#integral_primitive){reference-type="ref"
reference="integral_primitive"}, is Hodge and
$\psi_{\mathcal{E}}^{-1}(w)^2=w^2$ by Corollary
[42](#cor_2){reference-type="ref" reference="cor_2"}. If
$\mathrm{Pic}(Y)\cong \mathbb{Z}w$, then we deduce that
$\mathrm{Pic}(X)\cong \mathbb{Z}\psi_{\mathcal{E}}^{-1}(w)$, so we are
only left to prove that this class is ample. Recall that
$\psi_{\mathcal{E}}^{-1}$ sends some Kähler class on $Y$ to some Kähler
class on $X$, hence, it not only maps the positive cone in
$H^2(Y,\mathbb{Q})$ to the positive cone of $H^2(X,\mathbb{Q})$ but also
preserves the connected component containing Kähler classes. Therefore,
the class $\psi_{\mathcal{E}}^{-1}(w)$ is not anti-ample, hence is
ample. ◻
:::

The examples with $r=2r'\leq 4$ and $k\leq 5$ are listed as follows:
$$\begin{array}{cc|c}
        r&k&w^2\\
        \hline
        2&1&2(3-n)\\
        2&3&2(7-n)\\
        2&5&2(11-n)\\
        4&1&8(2-n)\\
        4&3&8(4-n)\\
        4&5&8(6-n),
    \end{array}$$ note that we consider only $n\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$
such that $w^2>0$. If $n=2$, the numerics on the first line give us the
EPW sextic and Theorem [37](#thm_main){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm_main"} together with Corollary
[44](#cor_div1){reference-type="ref" reference="cor_div1"} reads as
follows.

::: {#cor_EPWsextic .cor}
**Corollary 45** (EPW sextic). *Let
$(Y,w)\in {}^{2}\mathcal{M}_{1}^{(1)}$. Then, there is an ample divisor
$H$ on $Y$ and a connected component $X$ of the moduli space of
$H$-Gieseker semistable sheaves such that $X$ is of $K3^{[2]}$-type,
derived equivalent to $Y$ and parametrises $H$-slope stable modular
vector bundles $E$ with
$$\mathrm{rk}(E)=8, \qquad c_1(E)=4w \qquad \Delta(E)=\frac{16}{3}c_2(X).$$
Moreover, if $\mathrm{Pic}(Y)\cong \mathbb{Z}w$ then
$X\in {}^{2}\mathcal{M}_{1}^{(1)}$.*
:::

This example was already discussed in
[@kapustka-kapustka-derived-equivalent-hk4 Proposition 5.2], where it is
shown that the connected component of the moduli space $X$ can be taken
to be the dual EPW sextic. More precisely, in [@OG15 Section 4.2],
O'Grady shows that the correspondence between an EPW sextic and its dual
gives an automorphism of ${}^{2}\mathcal{M}_{1}^{(1)}$.

### Divisibility two

Let us fix a polarised IHS variety
$(Y,w)\in {}^{n}\mathcal{M}_{m}^{(2)}$ with polarisation of divisibility
two. This is non empty, irreducible of dimension 20 whenever
$n+m\equiv 1\pmod{4}$.

::: {#cor_div2 .cor}
**Corollary 46**. *Let $(Y,w)\in {}^{n}\mathcal{M}_{m}^{(2)}$ with
$n+m\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ and let us consider an odd integer
$r\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 3}$ such that $k:=w^2/(2r)\in \mathbb{Z}$ and
$\gcd(r,k)=1$. Then there there is a polarisation $H$ on $Y$ and a
connected component $X$ of the moduli space $M_{Y,H}$ of Gieseker
$H$-semistable sheaves on $Y$, such that*

- *$X$ parametrises $\mu_H$-stable modular vector bundles $E$ with
  $$rk(E)=r^nn! \qquad c_1(E)=r^{n-1}n!\dfrac{w}{2} \qquad \Delta(E)=\frac{(r^n n!)^2}{12}c_2(Y)$$*

- *$X$ and $Y$ are derived equivalent.*

*Moreover, if $\mathrm{Pic}(Y)\cong \mathbb{Z}w$ then
$(X,\psi_{\mathcal{E}}^{-1}(w))\in {}^{n}\mathcal{M}_{m}^{(2)}$.*
:::

The proof follows the same scheme as the one of Corollary
[44](#cor_div1){reference-type="ref" reference="cor_div1"}.

Some examples are listed below: $$\begin{array}{cc|c}
        r&k&w^2\\
        \hline
        3&1,2,4,5,\dots&6,12,24,30,\dots\\
        5&1,2,3,\dots &10,20,30,\dots\\
        7&1,2,3,\dots&14,28,42,\dots\\
        11&1,\dots&22,\dots\\
        19&1,\dots&38,\dots\\
    \end{array}$$ Let us observe that for any $n\geq 1$ and
$n\equiv 0,1,3\pmod{4}$ we have examples with $r=3, k=1,2,4$. Indeed,
the condition $n+m\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ becomes $n+rk\equiv 1\pmod{4}$, i.e.
$k\equiv n-1 \pmod{4}$. When $n\equiv 2\pmod{4}$ we can choose
$r=5, k=3$.

In the case of fourfolds, we have three explicit constructions of
locally complete families to which we can apply Theorem
[37](#thm_main){reference-type="ref" reference="thm_main"}, yielding the
following.

::: {#cor_BD_DV_IR .cor}
**Corollary 47** (Beauville--Donagi, Debarre--Voisin, Iliev--Ranestad).
*Let $(Y,w)$ be a polarised IHS manifold of $K3^{[2]}$-type such that
$\mathrm{div}(w)=2$ and one of the following holds:*

- *$w^2=6$,*

- *$w^2=22$,*

- *$w^2=38$.*

*Then there is an ample divisor $H$ on $Y$ and a connected component $X$
of the moduli space of Gieseker $H$-semistable sheaves such that $X$ is

- *$rk(E)=18,\quad c_1(E)=3h \quad \Delta(E)=27c_2(Y)$ in case $(a)$,*

- *$rk(E)=2\cdot11^2,\quad c_1(E)=11h\quad \Delta(E)=\frac{11^4}{3}c_2(Y)$
  in case $(b)$,*

- *$rk(E)=2\cdot19^2,\quad c_1(E)=19h,\quad \Delta(E)=\frac{19^4}{3}c_2(Y)$
  in case $(c)$.*

*Moreover, if $\mathrm{Pic}(Y)\cong \mathbb{Z}w$ then
$X\in {}^{2}\mathcal{M}_{w^2/2n}^{(2)}$.*
:::

## Hyperholomorphic vector bundles

In this Appendix, we prove that the fibers of a family of vector bundles
over some IHS manifold are projectively hyperholomorphic if the family
itself is projectively hyperholomorphic (see
Lemma [53](#lem_fibersarestable){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem_fibersarestable"}). For this purpose, we recall the
theory of (projectively) hyperholomorphic sheaves following Verbitsky
(see [@verbitsky-hyperholomorphic-sheaves] for a deeper discussion). We
refer the reader to [@markman_bbf] for a generalisation of Verbitsky's
results and to [@bottini-macri-stellari-hk-varieties] for an overview.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold endowed with a hyperkähler
structure (see [@verbitsky-hyperholomorphic-sheaves Definition 2.1]).
Thus, there exist complex structures $I,J,K\in\mathrm{End}(TM)$,
parallel with respect to $g$, satisfying the quaternionic relations
$$I^2=J^2=K^2=IJK=-\mathrm{id}_{TM}.$$ These endomorphisms induce an
action of the quaternion algebra $\mathbb{H}$ on the tangent bundle
$TM$, and hence of the group of unit quaternions, which is isomorphic to
$SU(2)$. Now, for every
$$L=aI+bJ+cK, \qquad a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}, \qquad a^2+b^2+c^2=1,$$ it
holds $L^2=-\mathrm{id}_{TM}$, so $L$ defines a complex structure on
$M$, and the metric $g$ is Kähler with respect to $L$. We denote by
$\omega_L$ the associated Kähler form. The set of induced complex
structures is naturally identified with the real sphere $S^2$.

::: rmk
*Remark 48*. The action of $SU(2)$ commutes with the Laplacian operator,
hence induces an action on cohomology (see
[@verbitsky-hyperholomorphic-sheaves Lemma 2.5]). Moreover, a
differential $2p$-form is $SU(2)$-invariant if and only if it is of
Hodge type $(p,p)$ with respect to every induced complex structure (see
[@verbitsky-hyperholomorphic-sheaves Lemma 2.6]).
:::

::: df
**Definition 49**. Let $E$ be a holomorphic vector bundle on the complex
manifold $(M,L)$.

1.  $E$ is called $\omega_{L}$-*slope stable hyperholomorphic* if it is
    $\omega_L$-slope stable and $c_i(E)\in H^{2i}(M,\mathbb{R})$ is
    $SU(2)$-invariant for $i=1,2$.

2.  $E$ is called $\omega_L$-*slope polystable hyperholomorphic* if it
    is $\omega_L$-slope polystable and each stable summand is
    $\omega_L$-slope stable hyperholomorphic.
:::

We will use the following characterization.

::: {#thm_hyperholocharacterization .thm}
**Theorem 50**. *A holomorphic vector bundle $E$ on $(M,L)$ is
$\omega_L$-slope polystable hyperholomorphic if and only if it admits a
hyperholomorphic connection, i.e. $E$ admits a hermitian metric such
that the curvature of the Chern connection is $SU(2)$-invariant.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* See [@verbitsky-hyperholomorphic-sheaves Theorem 3.19]. ◻
:::

::: {#def_proj_hyperhol .df}
**Definition 51**. A (possibly twisted) holomorphic vector bundle $E$ on
$(M,L)$ is *projectively $\omega_{L}$-slope stable hyperholomorphic* if
it is $\omega_L$-slope stable and $\mathcal{E}nd(E)$ is
$\omega_L$-polystable hyperholomorphic.
:::

### Stability of the fibers

We now prove Lemma [53](#lem_fibersarestable){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem_fibersarestable"}, which allows us to view the
projectively hyperholomorphic vector bundle
$\mathcal{E}\in \mathrm{Coh}(X\times Y,\alpha_\mathcal{E})$ constructed
in Theorem [15](#thm_compatiblevectorbundle){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm_compatiblevectorbundle"} as a family of stable vector
bundles on $Y$, parametrised by $X$. The key ingredient is the following
remark.

::: {#rmk_polyiffendpoly .rmk}
*Remark 52*. Let $(Y,\omega_Y)$ be a compact Kähler manifold with a
fixed Kähler class, and let $E$ be a holomorphic vector bundle. Then $E$
is $\omega_Y$-polystable if and only if $\mathcal{E}nd(E)$ is
$\omega_Y$-polystable. In fact, this follows from
[@anchouche-biswas-einstein-hermitian Corollary 3.8] by taking
$G = \mathrm{GL}_{\mathrm{rk}(E)}(\mathbb{C})$.
:::

Let now $(X,\omega_X)$ and $(Y,\omega_Y)$ be IHS manifolds with fixed
Kähler classes. In [@markman Section 5.3], it is explained how a
rational Hodge isometry
$H^2(X,\mathbb{Q}) \rightarrow H^2(Y,\mathbb{Q})$ sending $\omega_X$ to
$\omega_Y$ induces a diagonal hyperkähler structure on the real manifold
$M$ underlying $X \times Y$. Let
$\omega_{X\times Y} := \pi_X^*\omega_X \oplus \pi_Y^*\omega_Y$.

::: {#lem_fibersarestable .lem}
**Lemma 53**. *Let $(\mathcal{E},\alpha_{\mathcal{E}})$ be a
projectively $\omega_{X\times Y}$-stable hyperholomorphic vector bundle
such that $\alpha_Y = 0$, where we use the decomposition
$\alpha_\mathcal{E}= \alpha_X + \alpha_Y \in \mathrm{Br}(X\times Y) = \mathrm{Br}(X) \oplus \mathrm{Br}(Y)$.
Then for all $x \in X$, the fiber $\mathcal{E}|_{\{x\}\times Y}$ is
$\omega_Y$-slope polystable.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* We first observe that the condition $\alpha_Y=0$ implies that,
for every $x\in X$, the restriction $\mathcal{E}|_{\{x\}\times Y}$ is
untwisted. By assumption, the vector bundle $\mathcal{E}nd(\mathcal{E})$
is $\omega_{X\times Y}$-polystable and hyperholomorphic. Hence, by
Theorem [50](#thm_hyperholocharacterization){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm_hyperholocharacterization"}, it admits an hermitian
metric $h$ inducing a hyperholomorphic connection $\nabla$. The
restriction $h_x$ on $\mathcal{E}nd(\mathcal{E})|_{\{x\}\times Y}$ is
also hermitian, and we denote by $\nabla_x$ the induced Chern
connection. Since the hyperkähler structure on $X\times Y$ is diagonal,
the action of $SU(2)$ preserves the decomposition
$T_{X\times Y} = \pi_X^*T_X \oplus \pi_Y^*T_Y$. Consequently, the
curvature $F_{\nabla_x}$ is $SU(2)$-invariant - since $F_{\nabla}$ is -
hence
$\mathcal{E}nd(\mathcal{E}|_{\{x\}\times Y}) = \mathcal{E}nd(\mathcal{E})|_{\{x\}\times Y}$
also admits a hyperholomorphic connection. Again by
Theorem [50](#thm_hyperholocharacterization){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm_hyperholocharacterization"}, we deduce that
$\mathcal{E}nd(\mathcal{E}|_{\{x\}\times Y})$ is $\omega_Y$-slope
polystable. The result then follows from
Remark [52](#rmk_polyiffendpoly){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk_polyiffendpoly"}. ◻
:::

::: {#twistedmoduli .rmk}
*Remark 54*. It is worth observing that
Remark [52](#rmk_polyiffendpoly){reference-type="ref"
reference="rmk_polyiffendpoly"} remains valid in the twisted setting.
Let $E$ be a twisted vector bundle on a smooth projective manifold $Y$,
and fix a Kähler class $\omega_Y$. Then $E$ is $\omega_Y$-slope
polystable if and only if the untwisted vector bundle $\mathcal{E}nd(E)$
is $\omega_Y$-slope polystable. Indeed, by
[@connectionontwistedhiggsbundles Lemma 2.1], the twisted vector bundle
$E$ is $\omega_Y$-polystable if and only if the
$\operatorname{PGL}_r\times \mathbb{G}_m$-principal bundle
$\mathbb{P}(E)\times_Y(\det E)^{\otimes r}$ is $\omega_Y$-polystable as
a principal bundle (see also [@anchouche-biswas-einstein-hermitian
Definition 1.1]). On the other hand, by
[@anchouche-biswas-einstein-hermitian Corollary 3.8], the vector bundle
$\mathbb{P}(E)\times_Y(\det E)^{\otimes r}$ is $\omega_Y$-polystable if
and only if its adjoint bundle is $\omega_Y$-polystable. Since
$\operatorname{ad}(\mathbb{P}(E)\times_Y\det (E)^{\otimes r})\simeq \mathcal{E}nd(E)_0\oplus \mathcal{O}_Y\simeq \mathcal{E}nd(E)$,
the claim follows.

This observation allows one to prove
Lemma [53](#lem_fibersarestable){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem_fibersarestable"} without the assuming $\alpha_Y=0$.
Moreover, it suggests that the same construction in
Theorem [37](#thm_main){reference-type="ref" reference="thm_main"} can
also be used to exhibit components of moduli spaces of twisted sheaves
which are IHS manifolds of $K3^{[n]}$-type.
:::

## Variation of slope stability

In [@OGrady2026 Section 5], O'Grady constructs a wall-and-chamber
decomposition of the Kähler cone of an IHS manifold in order to study
variation of slope stability for modular sheaves. In the present paper,
we need an analogous statement, valid without the modularity assumption:
for a fixed family of torsion-free sheaves, the set of Kähler classes
with respect to which all fibres are slope-stable is open (see
Lemma [55](#lem_stability_open){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem_stability_open"}). Moreover, if this open subset is
nonempty, then it contains an ample class (see
Lemma [56](#lem_omegaimpliesH){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem_omegaimpliesH"}). We include short proofs of these two
facts in order to keep the paper self-contained, following arguments
along the lines of [@OGrady2026; @greb_ross_toma_moduli].

Let $Y$ be a projective IHS manifold. For $E,F\in\mathrm{Coh}(Y)$, we
let $$\lambda_{F,E}:=\mathrm{rk}(E)c_1(F)-\mathrm{rk}(F)c_1(E)$$ Let
$\omega\in H^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb{R})$ be a Kähler class. A torsion-free
coherent sheaf is $\omega$-slope stable if and only if for all coherent
subsheaves $0\subsetneq F\subsetneq E$ such that
$0<\mathrm{rk}(F)<\mathrm{rk}(E)$, we have
$$b_Y(\lambda_{F,E},\omega)<0,$$ where $b_Y$ is the BBF bilinear form
(see [@OGrady2026 Lemma 5.1]). For a Kähler class $\omega$, we set
$$S^{r,\Delta}_\omega := \left\{E\;\;\middle|\;
\begin{array}{c}
\text{$E$ is $\omega$-slope stable torsion-free sheaves} \\
\text{of rank $r$ and discriminant $\Delta$}
\end{array}
\right\}.$$

::: {#lem_stability_open .lem}
**Lemma 55**. *Let $Y$ be a projective IHS manifold and
$\omega\in H^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb{R})$ a Kähler class. Let
$r\in \mathbb{N}_{>0}$ and $\Delta\in H^4(Y,\mathbb{Z})$. Then the class
$\omega$ admits an open neighbourhood $V\subset\mathcal{K}_Y$ such that
for all $\omega'\in V$, we have
$S^{r,\Delta}_\omega\subset S^{r,\Delta}_{\omega'}$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Let $B\subset \mathcal{K}_Y$ be an open ball with center
$\omega$. Let $E\in S^{r,\Delta}_\omega$ and suppose it is unstable for
some $w'\in B$. By [@greb_toma Lemma 6.2] there is a $\bar{t}\in (0,1]$
such that $E$ is $\bar{t}\omega+(1-\bar{t})\omega'$-slope strictly
semistable. Hence, the path $t\omega+(1-t)\omega', t\in [0,1]$ must
cross a wall of the form
$$W_{F,E} = \{\alpha\in \mathcal{K}_Y |\;\;b_Y(\lambda_{F,E}, \alpha) = 0\; \}$$
where $F\subset E$ is maximally
$\bar{t}\omega+(1-\bar{t})\omega'$-destabilising (hence saturated).

We now show that only a finite number of such walls intersect $B$. It is
enough to show that there are only a finite number of
$\lambda_{F,E}\in \mathrm{NS}(Y)$, where $E\in S^{r,\Delta}_\omega$ and
$0\neq F\subsetneq E$ is a subsheaf with $\mathrm{rk}F<\mathrm{rk}E$
such that $b_Y(\lambda_{F,E}, \alpha)=0$ for some $\alpha\in B$.
Equivalently, picking a norm $\lVert \cdot\rVert$ on
$\mathrm{NS}(Y)_\mathbb{R}$, it is enough to prove: $$\sup \left\{ 
    \lVert \lambda_{F,E} \rVert 
    \;\middle|\; 
    \begin{aligned} 
        & E\in S^{r,\Delta}_\omega \\ 
        & E \text{ is } \alpha\text{-slope strictly semistable} \\[-0.5ex]
        & \text{for some } \alpha \in B, \text{ and } F \subset E \\[-0.5ex]
        & \text{is maximally destabilising} 
    \end{aligned} 
\right\} < \infty$$ In fact, we always have
$\lambda_{F,E}\in\mathrm{NS}(Y)$, which is discrete in
$\mathrm{NS}(Y)_\mathbb{R}$, and a discrete and bounded subset is
finite. Let us fix $\alpha, E,F$ be as above and consider $Q:=E/F$. By
[@OG22 Lemma 3.9] we have the following
$$\frac{\Delta(E)}{r_E}+\frac{\left(\lambda_{F,E}\right)^2}{r_Er_Fr_Q}=\frac{\Delta(F)}{r_F}+\frac{\Delta(Q)}{r_Q}$$
It is easy to check that both $F,Q$ are $\alpha$-slope semistable hence,
by Bogomolov inequality (see [@pavel_toma_survey Theorem 3.2]), we
obtain
$$\frac{\Delta(E)}{r_E}\cdot\alpha^{2n-2}+\frac{\left(\lambda_{F,E}\right)^2}{r_Er_Fr_Q}\cdot\alpha^{2n-2}=\frac{\Delta(F)}{r_F}\cdot\alpha^{2n-2}+\frac{\Delta(Q)}{r_Q}\cdot\alpha^{2n-2}\geq 0$$
Since $\alpha$ belongs to a relatively compact subset, the quantity
$\frac{\Delta(E)}{r_E}\cdot\alpha^{2n-2}$ is bounded from above, hence
there is a constant $C$ depending only on $r,\Delta$ and $B$, such that
$$-\left(\lambda_{F,E}\right)^2\cdot\alpha^{2n-2}< C.$$ By the Fujiki
identity, the positive constant $C':=\frac{(2n-2)!!}{2n-1}c_Y$ yields
the inequality
$$\left(\lambda_{F,E}\right)^2\cdot\alpha^{2n-2}=C'q_Y(\lambda_{F,E})q_Y(\alpha)^{n-1}.$$
Since $\overline{B}\subset\mathcal{K}_Y$ is compact, there exists
$\epsilon>0$, such that $q_Y(\alpha)>\epsilon$ for all $\alpha\in B$.
Combining this with the previous inequality, we obtain that there exists
a constant $C''$ only depending on $r,\Delta$ and $B$ such that
$$-q_Y(\lambda_{F,E})<C''$$ This immediately implies the claim that
$\lVert \lambda_{F,E}\rVert$ is uniformly bounded. In fact the signature
of the BBF form tells us that
$$m_\alpha=\min\{-q_Y(\beta)\;|\;\beta\in\alpha^\perp,\; \lVert \beta\rVert= 1\}$$
is positive, it depends continuously on $\alpha$ and $\alpha$ belongs to
a relatively compact subset, there exists $C'''>0$ depending only on $B$
such that $m_\alpha>C'''$. Note that we can assume $\lambda_{F,E}\neq 0$
hence we have
$$-q_Y(\lambda_{F,E})=-\lVert \lambda_{F,E}\rVert^2q_Y\left(\frac{\lambda_{F,E}}{\lVert \lambda_{F,E}\rVert}\right)>\lVert \lambda_{F,E}\rVert^2C'''$$
Combining the inequalities above, we get
$$\lVert \lambda_{F,E}\rVert^2<\frac{C''}{C'''}$$ obtaining the required
bound.

We have just showed that a finite number of walls intersect $B$. Hence
by choosing $V$ to be a ball with center $\omega$ and sufficiently small
radius we obtain the claim. ◻
:::

An immediate Corollary of the previous Lemma is the following.

::: {#lem_omegaimpliesH .lem}
**Lemma 56**. *Let $\omega\in\mathcal{K}_Y$. Then there exists
$H\in\mathrm{NS}(Y)$ ample such that
$S^{r,\Delta}_\omega\subset S^{r,\Delta}_{H}$.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* We decompose
$\omega = x + y \in H^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb{R}) = \mathrm{NS}(Y)_{\mathbb{R}} \oplus \big(T(Y)_{\mathbb{R}} \cap H^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb{R})\big)$.

We will now apply the Huybrechts--Boucksom criterion, [@boucksom
Théorème 1.2], to prove that $x$ also lies in $\mathcal{K}_Y$. In fact
$q_Y(\omega)=q_Y(x)+q_Y(y)$ and $T(Y)$ is negative definite, hence
$q_Y(\omega)>0$ implies that $q_Y(x)>0$. In particular, $x\neq 0$. We
consider the path $\omega_t=x+ty$. We observe that $q_Y(\omega_t)>0$ for
all $t\in [0,1]$: indeed,
$$q_Y(\omega_t)=q_Y(x)+t^2q_Y(y)\ge q_Y(x)+q_Y(y)=q_Y(\omega)>0,$$ hence
$x$ and $\omega$ are in the same connected component of the cone
$\{\alpha\in H^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb{R})|\;q_Y(\alpha)>0\}$. By the
Huybrechts-Boucksom criterion it suffices to check that for any rational
curve $C\subset Y$ we have $C.x\geq 0$. Since $y$ is transcendental, we
have $C.y=0$ hence $0\leq \omega.C=x.C+y.C=x.C$.

It is straightforward to check that
$S^{r,\Delta}_\omega\subset S^{r,\Delta}_{x}$. By Lemma
[55](#lem_stability_open){reference-type="ref"
reference="lem_stability_open"}, there exists
$x'\in\mathrm{NS}_{\mathbb{Q}}(Y)$ such that
$S^{r,\Delta}_{x}\subset S^{r,\Delta}_{x'}$. For an integer $m\gg 0$, we
have $H:=mx'\in\mathrm{NS}(Y)$ and it is ample. It follows that
$S^{r,\Delta}_{x}\subset S^{r,\Delta}_{x'}=S^{r,\Delta}_{H}$. ◻
:::
